apache-iceberg.wrapped_text:
Apache Iceberg
How does Iceberg work, and how do you use it? Start from Snowflake. One
product there owns three jobs: it stores the bytes, it tracks the table metadata,
and it runs the compute. Iceberg breaks those three jobs apart and standardizes
the middle one. Your rows sit in ordinary Parquet files in object storage that you
own. S3 is the common choice, but GCS, ADLS, HDFS, and MinIO work the
same way; Iceberg is not S3-native and uses no proprietary storage. Next to
those data files, Iceberg keeps a small set of metadata files. They record which
Parquet files form the table right now, the schema, the partition rules, and per-file
statistics such as row counts and column minimum and maximum values. That
metadata is the table format. Iceberg is a written specification, so it runs no
queries and stores no bytes itself.

Two external parts complete the picture. A catalog holds one pointer per table:
the location of the table's current metadata file. Each commit writes new files,
then swaps that pointer in one atomic step. This swap is what makes a write
ACID, and it is what gives you snapshots and time travel. Common catalogs are
the Iceberg REST catalog, AWS Glue, Apache Polaris, Project Nessie, Unity
Catalog, and Snowflake Open Catalog. An engine is the compute. It asks the
catalog for the pointer, reads the metadata, skips the files that cannot match the
query, and runs the SQL. Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, BigQuery, Athena, and
Snowflake can all act as the engine. The payoff is that several engines share one
copy of the data, with no exports and no copies. Your work stays SQL and
modeling, so a dbt model can materialize as an Iceberg table. You keep the
Snowflake behavior you expect, such as atomic commits, time travel, and
schema evolution, on files you own and any engine can read.

what-is-iceberg.wrapped_text:
What Is Iceberg?
Iceberg is a table format. It keeps a list of the exact files that
form a table at one point in time, together with the schema,
the partition rules, and per-file statistics. Because the file list
is explicit metadata, an engine knows the table content
without scanning storage, and a change becomes visible in
one atomic step.

What Is Iceberg?

table-format-vs-file-format.wrapped_text:
Table Format vs File Format
A file format defines how rows are stored inside one file.
Parquet, ORC, and Avro are file formats. A table format
defines which files belong to the table, what the columns
mean, and how a change is committed. Iceberg does not
replace Parquet; it organizes Parquet files into a table.

hive-style-table.wrapped_text:
Hive-Style Directory Table
In the older model, a directory path is the table and a
subdirectory is a partition. The engine must list
storage to find the data, so the listing is slow and
eventually inconsistent. There is no atomic commit, so
a reader can see a partly written result. Renaming a
column, or changing the partition layout, usually
needs a full rewrite.

iceberg-is-a-spec.wrapped_text:
Iceberg Is Only a Specification
Iceberg is not a query engine, not a storage system, and not a
database. It defines metadata files and rules. You still need an
engine to run queries, a catalog to hold the table pointer, and
object storage to hold the files.

Table Anatomy
The metadata forms a small tree.
One pointer in the catalog leads
to a metadata file, the metadata
file names a snapshot, the
snapshot names a manifest list,
and the manifest list names the
manifests that list the data
files.

catalog-pointer.wrapped_text:
Catalog Pointer
The catalog stores one value per table: the
location of the current metadata file. A
commit replaces that value. All readers start
here, so the pointer defines what the table is
right now.

metadata-file.wrapped_text:
Metadata File
The metadata file, usually a JSON file, holds
the table state: the schemas, the partition
specs, the sort orders, the table properties,
the list of snapshots, and which snapshot is
current. Each commit writes a new metadata
file instead of editing the old one.

table-schema.wrapped_text:
Schema
The schema lists the columns with a stable
field ID for each one. Engines match columns
by field ID, not by name or position. This is
why a rename does not break old data files.

Partition Spec
The partition spec defines how partition
values come from source columns, for example
`day(event_time)`. A table can hold several
specs, because the spec can change over time.
Each data file records which spec produced it.

snapshot.wrapped_text:
Snapshot
A snapshot is the complete set of data files
at one commit. It has an ID, a timestamp, a
summary of the operation, and a link to one
manifest list. Old snapshots stay in the
metadata file until you expire them.
snapshot.wrapped_original_text:

manifest-list.wrapped_text:
Manifest List
Each snapshot has one manifest list. It
names the manifests in the snapshot and, for
each one, the partition value ranges and the
file counts. This lets an engine skip whole
manifests before it reads them.
manifest-list.wrapped_original_text:

manifest-file.wrapped_text:
Manifest File
A manifest lists data files. For each file it
records the path, the partition values, the
row count, the file size, and column
statistics such as minimum, maximum, and null
counts. These statistics make file pruning
possible without opening the files.

data-files.wrapped_text:
Data Files
The data files hold the rows, normally as
Parquet, and sometimes as ORC or Avro. They
live in object storage such as S3, GCS, ADLS,
or HDFS. They are immutable: a writer adds new
files and never edits a committed one.

delete-files.wrapped_text:
Delete Files
A delete file marks rows as removed without
rewriting the data file. A position delete
names a file and the row positions inside it.
An equality delete names column values that
must disappear. Readers apply the delete files
that belong to the snapshot.

write-and-read-path.wrapped_text:
Write & Read Path
The write path shows how a change
becomes visible. The read path
shows how a query uses the
metadata to touch as few files as
possible.

write-plan.wrapped_text:
Writer Plans the Write
The engine reads the table pointer from the catalog
and loads the current metadata file. From it the
engine takes the schema, the current partition
spec, and the sort order it must follow.

write-data-files.wrapped_text:
Writer Writes Data Files
The engine writes the new rows into new data files
in storage. Nothing that already exists is changed,
so the current snapshot stays readable during the
write.

write-manifests.wrapped_text:
Writer Writes Manifests
The engine records the new files, with their
partition values and column statistics, in one or
more manifests. It then writes a manifest list for
the new snapshot, reusing the manifests that did
not change.

write-metadata-file.wrapped_text:
Writer Builds New Metadata File
The engine writes a new metadata file. It adds the
new snapshot, points the current snapshot at it,
and keeps the older snapshots in the list.

write-commit-swap.wrapped_text:
Catalog Swaps the Pointer
The catalog moves the table pointer from the
old metadata file to the new one in one atomic
operation. This swap is the commit. Until it
happens, the new files are invisible; after it
happens, they are fully visible.

Engine Asks the Catalog
The engine reads the table pointer and loads
the current metadata file. It never lists
storage directories to discover the table
content.

read-pick-snapshot.wrapped_text:
Engine Picks a Snapshot
Normally the engine uses the current snapshot,
so the whole query reads one consistent version.
A time-travel query selects an older snapshot by
ID or by timestamp instead.

read-prune-manifests.wrapped_text:
Engine Prunes Manifests
The engine compares the query filter against
the partition ranges in the manifest list.
Manifests that cannot hold a matching row are
skipped.
read-prune-manifests.wrapped_original_text:

read-prune-files.wrapped_text:
Engine Prunes Data Files
Inside the remaining manifests, the engine compares
the filter against each file's partition values and
column statistics. Files that cannot match are
skipped without being opened.

read-rows.wrapped_text:
Engine Reads Rows
The engine reads the surviving data files, and
reads only the needed columns. If the snapshot has
delete files that apply, the engine uses them to
drop the deleted rows from the result.

concurrency-control.wrapped_text:
Concurrency Control
Two writers can work at the same time, because
each one writes its own files and its own
metadata file. Only the pointer swap must be
serialized, and the catalog guarantees that.
The writer that loses the race revalidates its
change against the new current snapshot and
retries. Conflicts are therefore detected in
metadata, not by locking data files.

Two writers can work at the same time, because each one writes its own files and its own metadata file. Only the pointer swap must be serialized, and the catalog guarantees that. The writer that loses the race revalidates its change against the new current snapshot and retries. Conflicts are therefore detected in metadata, not by locking data files.

row-level-changes.wrapped_text:
Row-Level Changes
An update or a delete needs a decision:
rewrite the affected data files now, or record
the change and resolve it at read time. Both
options are valid, and a table can set them
per operation.

copy-on-write.wrapped_text:
Copy-on-Write
The writer rewrites every data file that holds
an affected row. Writes cost more, and reads
stay fast because there is nothing extra to
merge. This suits tables that change in large,
infrequent batches.

merge-on-read.wrapped_text:
Merge-on-Read
The writer keeps the data files and writes
delete files instead. Writes are fast, and
reads cost more because the engine must apply
the deletes. This suits frequent small
changes, and it needs regular compaction.

evolution-and-time-travel.wrapped_text:
Evolution & Time Travel
Because the table is described by
metadata, several changes that
once needed a rewrite become
metadata operations.
evolution-and-time-travel.wrapped_original_text:
Evolution & Time Travel
Because the table is described by metadata, several changes that once needed a rewrite become metadata operations.

schema-evolution.wrapped_text:
Schema Evolution
You can add, drop, rename, reorder, and widen
columns without rewriting data. Field IDs keep
the mapping stable, so an old file that lacks
a new column simply returns null for it.
Iceberg also prevents unsafe changes, such as
a type change that would lose data.

hidden-partitioning.wrapped_text:
Hidden Partitioning
The partition value is derived from a source
column by a transform recorded in the spec.
Queries filter on the real column, for example
`event_time`, and the engine derives the
partition itself. You do not add a separate
partition column, and a query does not break
when the partition rule changes.

partition-transforms.wrapped_text:
Partition Transforms
The common transforms are `identity`, `year`,
`month`, `day`, `hour`, `bucket(N, col)`, and
`truncate(N, col)`. Time transforms group rows
by period. `bucket` spreads values evenly by
hash, which suits high-cardinality keys.

Partitioning Still Needs Design
Hidden partitioning removes the extra column,
not the need to think. Too fine a granularity,
such as `hour` on a small table, creates many
tiny files and slow planning. Choose the
granularity from the data volume and the usual
query filters.

Partition Evolution
You can change the partition spec, for example
from `day` to `hour`, without rewriting
history. Old files keep the spec that produced
them, new files use the new spec, and the
engine plans across both.

time-travel.wrapped_text:
Time Travel
Because old snapshots stay listed in the
metadata file, you can query the table as it
was, by snapshot ID or by timestamp. This is
useful for audits, for comparing results,
and for debugging a bad load.

rollback.wrapped_text:
Rollback
Rollback sets the current snapshot back to
an earlier one. The bad commit stops being
visible, and no data file is rewritten. It
is the fastest repair after a wrong write.

Branches & Tags
A branch and a tag are named references to a
snapshot. A tag pins one snapshot, for example
a month-end version. A branch lets a writer
publish several commits away from the main
line, then merge or promote them.

Table Maintenance
A busy Iceberg table collects data
files, delete files, and metadata
files. Maintenance jobs keep
planning fast and storage cheap.
They are scheduled work; the
format does not do them for you,
although a managed service may.
table-maintenance.wrapped_original_text:

compaction.wrapped_text:
Compaction
Compaction rewrites many small data files into
fewer large ones, and can also merge delete
files into the data files. It usually re-sorts
the rows too, which tightens the column
statistics and improves pruning.
compaction.wrapped_original_text:

small-files-warning.wrapped_text:
Small Files Still Hurt
Iceberg tracks small files well, but it does
not merge them for you. Streaming writes and
frequent commits create many tiny files, which
slows planning and reading. Treat compaction
as a required job, not an optional one.

snapshot-expiry.wrapped_text:
Snapshot Expiry
Expiry removes old snapshots from the
metadata, then deletes the data files that
only those snapshots referenced. It controls
metadata size and storage cost, and it sets
how far back you can travel.
snapshot-expiry.wrapped_original_text:
Snapshot Expiry

expiry-not-backup.wrapped_text:
Expiry Is Not a Backup
Expiry deletes data permanently and shortens
the time-travel window. A rollback is
impossible once its snapshot is gone. Keep a
real backup, or a replicated copy, for
disaster recovery.

Orphan File Cleanup
A failed or aborted write can leave files in
storage that no metadata references. These
orphans cost money and are invisible to
queries. Cleanup compares storage against the
metadata and removes them, so it must use a
safe age threshold to avoid deleting files
from a write that is still running.

Manifest Rewrite
Many small commits leave many small manifests,
and pruning gets weaker. A manifest rewrite
regroups the file entries, usually by
partition, so the manifest list ranges stay
narrow and planning stays fast.

catalogs-and-engines.wrapped_text:
Catalogs & Engines
Iceberg needs two external roles:
a catalog that owns the table
pointer, and one or more engines
that read and write the files.

catalog-role.wrapped_text:
Catalog Role
The catalog maps a table name to its current
metadata file, and it performs the pointer
swap as one atomic operation. It also holds
namespaces, and it is often where access
control lives. Without a catalog there is no
safe commit, because two writers could
overwrite each other. The catalog stays
deliberately thin: it owns the pointer, the
names, and the permissions, not the table
metadata itself.

The catalog stays deliberately thin: it owns the pointer, the names, and the permissions, not the table metadata itself.

common-catalogs.wrapped_text:
Common Catalogs
The Iceberg REST catalog is an open API that a
client can talk to, and several products
implement it: Apache Polaris, Project Nessie,
Lakekeeper, and the catalog services of the
cloud and lakehouse vendors. Other widely used
options are the AWS Glue Data Catalog, the
Hive Metastore, Databricks Unity Catalog,
Snowflake Open Catalog, a JDBC catalog backed
by a relational database, and the filesystem
catalog, which is easy to start with but weak
for concurrent writers.

Engine Role
An engine uses an Iceberg client library to
resolve the pointer, plan the scan, prune
files, and read or write data. Iceberg itself
runs no compute. Because the table state is in
shared metadata, several engines can use one
table without copying it.

Common Engines
Apache Spark and Apache Flink are the usual writers, and Flink covers streaming ingestion. Trino, Presto, Dremio, Apache Impala, StarRocks, ClickHouse, and DuckDB are common query engines. Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Amazon Athena read Iceberg tables as well, and some of them can also manage and write them.

metadata-not-in-catalog.wrapped_text:
Metadata Is Not in the Catalog
The metadata file, the manifest list, and the
manifests are real files in your object
storage, beside the data files. The catalog
stores only the path of the current metadata
file. This split exists because only the
pointer needs atomic replacement; everything
else is immutable, so engines read it straight
from storage in parallel. Two cases blur the
line. A catalog can return the metadata
contents to a client, because it read the file
for you, and it may cache them; the file stays
the source of truth. A managed service can
also hide the files from view, but they still
exist in your storage. If you come from a
warehouse, expect the word to mislead you:
there a catalog is a rich metadata service,
here it is a pointer holder.
